title: Data tidying
summary: Use tidyr to reshape bike trip tables and survey data. Make tables longer, split mixed column names, and turn summaries into wide reports.

steps.title: Setup: library(tidyverse)

runs.purpose: load the tidyverse, which includes tidyr

steps.explain: `library(tidyverse)` attaches tidyr, whose `pivot_longer()` and `pivot_wider()` this lesson uses, along with readr and dplyr.

steps.title: Tidy data, and a table that isn't

runs.purpose: read the trips started at each station in each month of 2025 into `months`
runs.task: Read `data/station-months.csv` into a variable called `months` with `read_csv()`.

steps.explain:
Data is tidy when each variable is a column, each observation is a row, and each value is a cell. `months` is laid out for people to read instead: one row for each of {n_stations} stations, with the month, a variable, spread over twelve column names from `jan` to `dec`.

The number of trips, a single variable, fills twelve columns. To total each month, or to chart the year, the month needs to be a column of its own.

steps.title: Lengthen: pivot_longer()

runs.code:
months |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = jan:dec,
    names_to = "month",
    values_to = "trips"
  )
runs.purpose: turn the twelve month columns into rows: one column for the month, one for the trips
runs.task: Make `months` longer with `pivot_longer()`. Stack `jan` to `dec`; put their names in `month` and values in `trips`.

runs.code:
monthly <- months |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = jan:dec,
    names_to = "month",
    values_to = "trips",
    values_drop_na = TRUE
  )
alternatives: monthly = months |> pivot_longer(jan:dec, names_to = 'month', values_to = 'trips') |> filter(!is.na(trips))
runs.purpose: do the same without the empty cells, and keep it as `monthly`
runs.task: Do the same again, adding `values_drop_na = TRUE`, and store the result in `monthly`.

steps.explain:
`pivot_longer()` makes a table longer. `cols` picks the columns to stack, `names_to` names the new column their names go into, and `values_to` the one their values go into. Each station now has a row per month: {n_long} rows of station, month and trips.

{n_na} of them have no count: all twelve months of the two Saltings stations, where no trip started in 2025. `values_drop_na = TRUE` leaves those cells out, so `monthly` has {n_monthly} rows.

steps.title: Long data is easy to work with

values.peak_month: local({s <- summarize(monthly, trips = sum(trips), .by = month); s$month[which.max(s$trips)]})
values.low_month: local({s <- summarize(monthly, trips = sum(trips), .by = month); s$month[which.min(s$trips)]})

runs.purpose: total the trips in each month, across all stations
runs.task: Total the `trips` for each `month` in `monthly`, with `summarize()` and `.by`.

values.peak_top: local({s <- summarize(monthly, trips = sum(trips), .by = month); slice_max(filter(monthly, month == s$month[which.max(s$trips)]), trips)$name[1]})
values.peak_top_trips: local({s <- summarize(monthly, trips = sum(trips), .by = month); format(max(filter(monthly, month == s$month[which.max(s$trips)])$trips))})

runs.purpose: find the busiest station in each month
runs.task: Find the station with the most `trips` in each `month`, with `slice_max()` and its `by` argument.

steps.explain:
With one column of months and one of trips, a question about months is one verb. The busiest month was {peak_month}, with {peak_trips} trips; the quietest was {low_month}, with {low_trips}. `slice_max()` keeps the row with the most trips in each month, {n_slices} rows: in {peak_month} that was {peak_top}, with {peak_top_trips} trips.

In the wide table, each of these would need twelve columns named one by one.

steps.title: Two variables in each name: names_sep

runs.purpose: read the trips started at each station on weekdays and weekends, before and after noon, into `periods`

runs.code:
periods |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = !station_id,
    names_to = c("day", "half"),
    names_sep = "_",
    values_to = "trips"
  )
alternatives: periods |> pivot_longer(weekday_am:weekend_pm, names_to = c('day', 'half'), names_sep = '_', values_to = 'trips')
runs.purpose: stack the four count columns, splitting each name into the kind of day and the half of the day
runs.task: Make `periods` longer. Stack every column except `station_id`. Split names at `_` into `day` and `half`; call the values `trips`.

steps.explain:
Each name in `periods`, such as `weekday_am`, holds two variables: the kind of day, and whether the trip started before noon (`am`) or after (`pm`). Given two names in `names_to`, `pivot_longer()` splits each column name at `names_sep` and puts the parts in `day` and `half`. `cols = !station_id` picks every column except `station_id`.

Station 101 had {first_am} weekday trips before noon and {first_pm} after, now in two rows instead of two columns.

steps.title: Part of a name is a column: .value

runs.purpose: read each station's trips and median trip length for members and casual riders into `riders`

runs.code:
riders |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = !station_id,
    names_to = c(".value", "member_type"),
    names_sep = "_"
  )
runs.purpose: make one row per station and rider type, with a column for trips and one for minutes
runs.task: Make `riders` longer. Split names at `_`; keep the first part as a column name with `.value`. Put the second part in `member_type`.

steps.explain:
`riders` has two measurements, `trips` and `minutes` (the median trip length), each for two rider types: `trips_member`, `minutes_casual` and so on. The first part of each name is a variable's name, not a value.

`.value` in `names_to` tells `pivot_longer()` to make that part a column, so the result has `trips` and `minutes` side by side, and `member_type` from the second part: {n_riders} rows, two per station. At station 101, members made {m_trips} trips with a median of {m_min} minutes; casual riders made {c_trips}, with a median of {c_min}.

steps.title: One row per answer: names_prefix

runs.code:
uses <- survey |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("use_"),
    names_to = "use",
    names_prefix = "use_",
    values_drop_na = TRUE
  )
alternatives: uses = survey |> pivot_longer(starts_with('use_'), names_to = 'use', names_prefix = 'use_') |> filter(!is.na(value))
runs.purpose: make one row for each use a rider ticked, and keep it as `uses`
runs.task: Make `survey` longer. Stack columns starting with `use_`; remove that prefix with `names_prefix` and call the new column `use`. Leave out empty cells. Store the result in `uses`.

runs.purpose: count how many riders ticked each use
runs.task: Count the rows for each `use`, most first.

steps.explain:
The survey asked what riders use the bikes for, and they could tick any of five answers. Each answer has its own column, `use_commuting` to `use_visiting`, holding Yes or nothing. Longer, `uses` has one row for each ticked answer: {n_uses} rows from {n_survey} responses.

`names_prefix` takes `use_` off each name, and `values_drop_na = TRUE` leaves out the answers not ticked. Counting is now one step: {top_use} was ticked most, {top_n} times.

steps.title: Widen for a report: pivot_wider()

runs.code:
uses |>
  count(use, member_type) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = member_type, values_from = n)
runs.purpose: count each use for members and casual riders, then give each rider type its own column
runs.task: Count `uses` by `use` and `member_type`. Use `pivot_wider()` to make one column per `member_type`, filled from `n`.

steps.explain:
`pivot_wider()` does the opposite of `pivot_longer()`: `names_from` is the column whose values become column names, and `values_from` is the one that fills them.

The result is a report with one row for each use and a column for each rider type: members ticked commuting {m_commute} times, casual riders {c_commute}, while casual riders ticked leisure {c_leisure} times. Wide tables suit people reading them; long, tidy ones suit R working on them.
